summary:
Future Farm compares three crop rotations for an irrigated farm in Fallon, Nevada, using NASA POWER weather. A playable farm simulator shows how each rotation scores on water, heat and soil health, why it ranks where it does, and how stable that ranking is when rain, warming and farmer priorities change.
Links
• Code: https://github.com/FarrahTharwat/future-farm
• Live: https://wealthy-stop-tk9bz.ship.place/
• Video: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1IX7CiV2GFYom3o6Z9sAIn40t8bIFti5q/view?usp=share_link
details:
What it does

A farmer in Fallon, Nevada has to decide what to grow on irrigated land where water is limited. Future Farm compares three rotations side by side: the current alfalfa stand (the baseline), Alternative A, a water-conserving rotation of small grains and field pea, and Alternative B, a soil-health rotation with corn silage, a legume and winter cover crops. Each rotation is scored on water, climate and soil health. The simulator shows the three farms through the seasons, lets you move rain and warming sliders, and explains every score.

Why a comparison tool and not a recommendation

The scores are close, and the inputs are not yet verified by local experts. So the tool does not say what to grow. It shows the tradeoffs, how stable they are, and where the answer would change, so a farmer or adviser can decide what matters.

How it works

It is a transparent rule-based calculation (multi-criteria decision analysis), not a trained model. No labelled data says which rotation improved which field, so a trained model could not be validated. Every number can be traced to an input and a formula.

  • Water: each crop's need is its crop coefficient times reference evapotranspiration over its growing days (FAO-56 method), minus usable rain, compared with an assumed irrigation supply of 1,220 mm a year.
  • Climate: the share of growing days above each crop's heat limit, from NASA POWER daily maximum temperature for 2001 to 2025, weighted by how far above the limit each day is.
  • Soil health: a checklist of potential benefits (nitrogen-fixing crops, green cover, roots and residue, crop variety). It is not a measurement of soil.
  • Overall: a weighted sum with illustrative default weights of 40% water, 25% climate and 35% soil health. Each criterion's contribution is the explanation.
  • Stress test: 20% less rain and 1.5 C warmer, shown beside the ranking, not inside it.
  • Stability: the priorities are swept to find the point where the top rotation changes, and the model is rerun in 27 cases that vary water demand, heat limits and how severely heat days are weighted.

What we found

  • The current alfalfa rotation scores highest (61.4). Alternatives A and B are tied at 57.4, so the tool shows them as tied.
  • Alternative A needs about 158 mm a year less irrigation than the current rotation (616 against 774 mm) but has the most heat-stress days and the lowest soil-health score.
  • The current rotation ranks first in all 27 uncertainty cases, but its lead can shrink to about 1 point under assumptions that favour the alternatives.
  • Alternative A takes the lead only if water is weighted above about 54.5%, compared with 40% by default.

Honest limits

This is a prototype. Crop values come from public sources (FAO-56, UNR Extension, NRCS) and have not been checked by local experts. Heat limits and soil ratings are estimates. Reference evapotranspiration comes from a Fallon weather-station average, not from NASA data. In the current rotation, alfalfa establishment overlaps with the end of the previous winter wheat, which an outside review estimates overstates the baseline's irrigation by roughly 90 mm a year (unverified). Frost and soil salinity are not modelled. The tool is meant to support local expertise, not replace it.

Next steps

Validate crop values with UNR Extension in Churchill County, replace the station evapotranspiration with a NASA-derived series, add SMAP, SoilGrids and MODIS data, and apply the tool to other regions. The model accepts any coordinates, but crops, calendars and water rules would need to be replaced for each region.

Space agency data

  • NASA POWER (daily point data, 2001 to 2025, at 39.47 N, 118.78 W): maximum temperature drives the climate score, precipitation drives the rain term in the water score, and mean temperature scales evapotranspiration in the warming scenarios.
  • NASA SMAP surface soil moisture: explored as a regional cross-check, but the downloaded series was too short to compare with the model, so it is not used. It is listed as a next step.

Use of artificial intelligence

The team made the design decisions and ran all of the code. An AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic) was used to help draft and review code, explain methods and write documentation. Explanations in the simulator are template sentences built from the numbers in the results file, not generated live.

Hackathon journey

We started with a broad idea and narrowed it to a transparent comparison of three rotations for one farm. Along the way we dropped SHAP and a live language model, because a weighted sum already explains itself. We removed climate resilience from the overall score after realising it counted the same information twice, and made it a separate stress test. We added an uncertainty analysis and a tie flag when the first results showed two rotations almost level, so the tool would not show a false ranking. SMAP and MODIS data did not arrive in a usable form in time, so we documented them as next steps.

References

  • Allen, R.G., Pereira, L.S., Raes, D., Smith, M. (1998). Crop evapotranspiration, FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56.
  • NASA POWER Project, daily point API (community AG).
  • USBR AgriMet, station FALN (Fallon, NV), monthly reference evapotranspiration, 2001 to 2010.
  • UNR Extension fact sheets and trials on alfalfa, teff and cover crops in Nevada.
  • USDA-NRCS Great Basin Plant Materials Center, Fallon: cool-season cover crop evaluation.
  • FAO ECOCROP crop data sheets.
  • Full register with verification status: data/agricultural/agronomy_sources.md in the repository.
